Introduction:
The effect of in-person school on COVID-19 case rates in the USA has been heavily debated, although establishing causality is fraught with challenges.

Estimating this relationship requires confronting at least three statistical obstacles. First, different areas closed schools at different times, at least partly in response to community case rates [ 1 ]. This makes it difficult to disentangle the causal effects of school closures on cases. Second, schools may have opened at times that coincided with community waves, thus creating a spurious impression that the former caused the latter. Third, measured case rates depend heavily on the extent of testing, but the availability and use of tests varied across age groups, regions, and time. Testing was also correlated with political attitudes, which may have driven other pandemic responses [ 2 ].

We address these challenges using three novel approaches. First, rather than relying purely on spatial variation across areas that opened or closed schools, we study the Fall of 2021 when schools in all 50 US states opened for regular in-person learning following summer break. This allows us to exploit exogenous variation in the timing of school openings as opening dates are based on long-standing school calendars. For example, schools in the South typically open multiple weeks before schools in the Northeast.

Second, we employ restricted data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to directly account for community case rates. Therefore, even if school opening coincided with a local wave of cases, this will be controlled for by our measure of community transmission.

Third, although systematic nationwide data on testing by age group do not exist, we obtained data from four jurisdictions on age-stratified COVID-19 testing rates. Using these data we examine whether differential testing rates may have been a confounder in previous studies from the USA and the UK finding higher COVID-19 case rates associated with school reopening [ 3–7 ].

By contrast, research from other countries provides some evidence that open schools were not associated with increased cases, including from Australia [ 8 , 9 ], Germany [ 10 , 11 ], Ireland [ 12 ], Japan [ 13 ], Brazil [ 14 ], the Nordic countries [ 15–17 ], and in meta-analyses [ 18–20 ].

The USA is provides an opportune setting to examine this question, as school policies are set at either the state or local level, with at least 50 jurisdictions across which to compare interventions and outcomes can be compared. Notably, prior US studies examine the 2020–21 school year, comparing areas with closed versus open schools [ 3–6 , 21 , 22 ]. However, as Bravata et al [ 3 ] note, “[C]omparing COVID-19 cases between reopened and non-reopened schools…is likely to lead to biased results.” Additionally, most prior US studies do not separate out pediatric and adult cases or consider that testing rates can be an important confounder. If there is a lower threshold for testing children for SARS-CoV-2 when schools are in session, this may create a spurious association between schools and higher COVID-19 case rates.
Methods:
We examined school openings in the USA in the Fall of 2021, following the summer break. Our study period was 1 August to 15 December 2021, which was the first time during the COVID-19 pandemic that schools in all 50 states opened according to their regular schedule. Had we examined the 2020–21 school year instead, as done by all prior US studies, the results would likely be confounded by certain states or districts choosing to close in response to case rates, especially as the CDC discouraged opening schools during periods of high transmission [ 1 ]. We end the study period on 15 December, because the Omicron wave caused a shortage of testing in some areas [ 23 ]—which would have undercounted cases—and further disrupted schools in January 2022.

### Data and sample

We obtain county-level COVID-19 case rates from the Restricted Case Dataset provided by the CDC. We obtain school opening dates from the data provider MCH, which has been used in similar studies in the past [ 24 , 25 ]. County demographic data were obtained from the US Census Bureau and pediatric vaccination rates from the US Department of Health and Human Services. Of the 3104 counties in the USA, we obtained complete data from 2592 counties, containing over 86% of the US population. The supplementary material contains additional information on data sources and sample construction.

The data range from 3 weeks prior to school opening until 12 weeks following, for a total of 16 weeks. The starting date of 3 weeks prior follows past studies [ 24 , 25 ]. The 12-week end date is the latest possible date with complete data for all counties.

### Statistical analysis

We estimate linear regressions of COVID-19 cases per capita among children (ages 0–19) on adult cases per capita in each county and week. We include a large set of control variables; details are in the supplementary material .

We exploit the temporal variation in school opening dates across the USA by including fixed-effects for each week prior to or following school opening. In each county, we define Week 0 as the week of school opening, with Week −1 the week prior and so on.

These school-week fixed-effects represent our main outcome measure as they are estimates of pediatric cases per capita in the corresponding school-week, holding constant adult cases, demographic characteristics, and vaccination rates. We normalize to zero the fixed-effect for 3 weeks prior to opening. Therefore, all coefficients are interpreted as the increase in pediatric case rates relative to rates in adults, for the corresponding school-week compared to 3 weeks prior to the start of school.

Note that, as all schools reopened for in-person learning in the Fall of 2021, there is no control group of schools that did not open. Thus, our analysis is a timing-based event study [ 26 ], as it exploits differences in the timing of school opening, rather than a cross-sectional comparison of districts which would lend itself to a difference-in-differences type analysis.

The supplementary material presents more details on the empirical specification and alternative results to assess robustness.

### Testing

An important potential confounder is that the COVID-19 testing threshold among children may be correlated with school opening due to public health measures. For example, policies such as “Test-to-Stay” required automatic testing of children, with a minimum of two tests per child, in a classroom with a known case of COVID-19 [ 27 , 28 ]. Additionally, some families may have voluntarily tested their children due to concerns about infections in schools. Both these factors would have caused children to be tested at higher rates, relative to adults, once schools reopened. This higher rate of testing may have mechanically increased reported cases even if schools were not the source of exposures. Therefore, it is important to consider rates of COVID-19 testing among children as a potential confounder.

There is no source that provides data on age-stratified testing for the entire country. We obtained data from four jurisdictions: the states of New York, Florida and Georgia, and the city of Chicago. All of these report testing rates and confirmed cases based on laboratory reports, separately for various age categories. The supplementary material provides data definitions, sources, and the full list of jurisdictions that were searched. We use these data to examine whether testing rates rose in children after schools opened, and then adjust the regression estimates to account for differential rates of testing.

### Mitigations in schools

Additional confounding may have been introduced by variation in public health measures to mitigate transmission when schools reopened. Some prior studies suggest that such measures may reduce transmission in schools [ 29–31 ]. To account for this, we control for county-level school mask mandates in the statistical analysis. Mask mandates should be a good proxy for other public health interventions, as areas which mandated masks in schools also tended to introduce other interventions [ 24 ].
Results:
Aggregate results for the entire country are presented in Fig. 1 . The figure plots school-week fixed effects, and the associated 95% confidence interval, normalizing the value for 3 weeks prior to opening to zero. Fig. 1 suggests that case rates in children, relative to adults, rise in the period surrounding the opening of school, peak in the second week after school opening, and then decline steadily. At the peak, there are an average of 39.3 [37.7, 40.9] additional cases per 100 000 children relative to adults, compared to the rate 3 weeks prior to school opening.

Fig. 2 stratifies the aggregate result for each of the four Census regions in the USA and indicates the national pattern is replicated in all regions of the country.

Fig. 3 stratifies the aggregate data from Fig. 1 by presence or absence of school mask mandates. Case rates decline after the first 2 weeks of school in both groups of counties with no significant difference in case rates.

For all the above results, the supplementary material presents various robustness exercises. These include defining the dependent variable as either the ratio of pediatric to adult cases or the total number of cases, and further stratifying the country into the nine Census divisions. The pattern of results shown thus far is repeated in these additional tests.

Fig. 4 presents data on cases and testing for the four jurisdictions with age-stratified testing data. The dashed black line in each sub-plot corresponds to the median week of school opening in each jurisdiction. This ranges from Week 31 (August 2) in Georgia to Week 36 (September 6) in New York.

Fig. 4 suggests that pediatric testing rates, relative to the total population, rose considerably after schools opened, with 91%–98% correlation (r) between testing rates and case rates in children, relative to adults.

Table 1 presents the average fraction in children of both tests and cases, separately for 6-week periods prior to and following the start of school. The proportion of tests done in children rises by 10% (from 12% to 22%) between these periods, and the proportion of reported cases rises by 8% (15% to 23%), suggesting a lower threshold for testing children after schools reopened.

Fig. 5 shows reported cases of COVID-19 in children adjusted for testing rates with a blue dashed line. Compared with the red line, which is not adjusted for testing, the test-adjusted case rates are considerably lower ( P < .01 for all coefficients except Week 12), with a peak of 19 additional cases per 100 000 children.

Once rates of testing are adjusted for, case rates among schoolchildren are lower, by 10.65 [3.9, 17.6] cases per 100 000 students, after 3 weeks of school, than they were prior to schools opening. When comparing all weeks that schools were open, rates were lower by 4.7 cases per 100 000 ( P < .01) than before schools opened.

Finally, in Fig. 6 , we present data from the CDC on hospitalization rates among children in 13 states for which information is available, including the states of Georgia and New York [ 32 ]. Fig. 6 shows no clear relationship between school opening dates and the rate of pediatric hospitalizations for COVID-19.
Discussion:
Our study shows that school openings in the USA coincided with an initial rise in recorded pediatric cases of COVID-19, relative to adult cases in the community, followed by a steady decline ( Figs 1–3 ). However, schoolchildren were tested at significantly higher rates when schools were in session ( Fig. 4 , Table 1 ). When testing rates are taken into account, we find that school opening was associated with significantly lower case rates among children for at least the first 12 weeks of the 2021–22 academic year ( Fig. 5 ).

While it is possible the increased pediatric testing rate that coincided with school opening was driven by a higher SARS-CoV-2 disease burden, multiple lines of evidence suggest otherwise. First, we find testing of children rose more than it did for the population at large when schools reopened with over 90% correlation. In the supplementary material , we control for additional testing variables ( Fig. S4 ) with consistent results. Second, CDC data ( Fig. 6 ) along with data from multiple countries [ 20 ] fail to find a clear rise in pediatric or adult COVID-19 hospitalizations following school reopening. Third, wastewater analysis from 2022 also suggests that school openings had little to no relationship with case rates across the USA [ 33 ].

Fourth, school-based public health policies implemented in the USA during the COVID-19 pandemic encouraged testing for SARS-CoV-2. For example, the CDC recommended weekly SARS-CoV-2 screening testing for K-12 students beginning in Spring of 2021, unless community transmission was “low” [ 34 ]. Additionally, though not yet officially recommended by the CDC in the Fall of 2021, “Test-to-Stay” had already been widely adopted [ 27 , 28 , 35 ] by the Fall of 2021, which would have triggered multiple tests of entire classes with a positive case [ 27 ]. These initiatives would have encouraged a lower threshold for testing students, likely capturing infections among other children who would not otherwise have been tested or included in case numbers.

We attempted to resolve this confounding by adjusting for the observed number of tests in children in four jurisdictions and find support for both hypotheses ( Fig. 5 ). Controlling for the number of tests significantly reduces the relative spike in cases among children when schools reopen, suggesting that the relative increase in pediatric cases may have been mechanically driven by increased testing rates.

However, even after controlling for testing rates, Fig. 5 shows a brief rise in pediatric cases around the start of school that appears to begin even prior to school reopening. One possible explanation is that the start of school terms coincides with the end of summer vacations and a significant change in routines and networks. Travel, summer camps, and other activities may cause children to be in different networks during the summer than when they return to school. Once schools have been in session for 2 or more weeks, the regular routine may lead children to be less exposed to members of networks different from their own, possibly explaining the decline in case rates over time.

Our results do not support the hypothesis that in-person schooling is responsible for driving up overall infection rates among children. In all specifications, and regardless of whether we control for testing rates, case rates decline quickly once schools have been open for more than 2 weeks. Moreover, once testing rates and community case rates are adjusted for, COVID-19 case rates among children were significantly lower after around 3 weeks of schools being in session than during the summer break ( Fig. 5 ).

Our findings of low or even negative correlation of school opening with COVID-19 transmission among children are consistent with multiple international studies [ 8–17 ]. However, they are inconsistent with studies from the USA which thus far have not adjusted for testing rates [ 3–6 ].

We also show that school mask mandates do not affect the results, which is consistent with randomized studies on masking [ 36 ], and some prior observational studies [ 24 , 37 , 38 ]. This does not necessarily mean that masks are ineffective in general; schoolchildren may perhaps be less likely to comply with mask wearing for the entire school day compared with adults in other settings. Moreover, our study was not designed to evaluate the effectiveness of school mask mandates.

We also acknowledge some limitations of our study. First, this study is observational and cannot definitively rule out a link between school openings and increased cases. Nevertheless, a strong causal link is unlikely, given that we account for both spatial and temporal effects, as well for confounders such as testing and non-pharmaceutical interventions. Establishing or ruling out causal effects may require a randomized controlled trial of school closures, as was suggested in Norway [ 39 ].

Second, our results depend on reported cases and rates of testing, both of which are subject to error. For example, our data on testing are based on laboratory tests, which vary by jurisdiction and do not include home tests.

Third, while our analysis of age-stratified testing rates is novel, and addresses an important confounder in past studies, it uses data from just four jurisdictions, which may not be representative of the entire country.

Fourth, while we find little evidence school openings drive up pediatric infections, we acknowledge that school closures may have been intended to reduce severe disease in at risk adults. While this study focuses on outcomes in children, we present a robustness exercise in the supplementary material ( Fig. S6 ) that shows that total community cases among adults and children followed a similar pattern to the one established so far, which is consistent with other studies [ 14 , 20 ].

Finally, the data only permit us to examine children aged 0–19, not all of whom are in the school system, though we note that testing was encouraged or required in daycares and college as well [ 40 , 41 ].

Our study also has several strengths and novel features. First, it is the largest observational study to date of the relationship between schools and pediatric COVID-19 cases, encompassing over 86% of the US population. Second, by exploiting both temporal and spatial variation in school opening dates, it avoids the problem of selection bias in studies that rely only on a spatial comparison of areas that kept schools open or closed.

Third, this is the first study to incorporate age-stratified data on testing, which is likely to be a major confounder in prior studies. Rates of testing are strongly correlated with the dates of school opening, suggesting that studies which ignore this variable may over-estimate the effect of schools on case rates.
Conclusion: In the Fall of 2021, COVID-19 case rates among children, relative to the community, rose briefly around the start of school, but returned to baseline within a month. However, children were tested at significantly higher rates when schools were in session. Once testing rates were adjusted for, COVID-19 case rates among children were significantly lower, relative to community rates, after 3 weeks of in-person schooling. These findings refute the notion that school reopening led to increased SARS-CoV-2 transmission in the 2021–22 academic year.
